H1.text: Take three plus two i, and three minus two i. Both numbers carry an imaginary part.

H2.text: Add them, and you get six. Multiply them, and you get thirteen. Every i has vanished.

H3.text: Aarav saw the same idea on his ride home today.

H4.text: His friend Ravi waited exactly opposite, across the road. Same distance along, just on the other side of the middle line.

H5.text: Complex numbers have partners like that. Today: when are two complex numbers equal, and what is a conjugate?

E1.text: First question. When are two complex numbers equal?

E2.text: Every complex number has two parts: a real part, a, and an imaginary part, b, next to i.

E3.text: Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match. Real with real, imaginary with imaginary.

E4.text: Watch the match test. Three plus two i, against three plus two i. Real parts match. Imaginary parts match. Equal.

E5.text: Now three plus two i, against three minus two i. The real parts match, but the imaginary parts do not. Not equal.

E7.text: So one complex equation gives two real equations. That is the power of equality.

C1.text: Now, the partner from the hook.

C2.text: The conjugate of a plus i b is a minus i b.

C3.text: Keep the real part. Flip the sign of the imaginary part. That is all.

C4.text: We write it as z with a bar on top, and read it as z bar.

C5.text: Watch z move. Its conjugate follows, like a reflection in the real axis, the middle line.

C6.text: When z climbs up, z bar dips down. Real parts stay equal. Imaginary parts stay opposite.

C7.text: And when z lands on the middle line, the two meet. A real number is its own conjugate.

K1.text: Quick one. Is six i its own conjugate, like a real number? Pause and think.

K2.text: No! Six i is zero plus six i, so its conjugate is minus six i. Only real numbers are their own conjugates.

S1.text: Side by side. The conjugate flips one sign. Three plus two i becomes three minus two i: a mirror image across the line.

S2.text: The negative flips both signs. Three plus two i becomes minus three minus two i, through the centre.

S3.text: Now you try. What is the conjugate of four minus seven i? Pause and decide.

S4.text: Four plus seven i! Keep the real part. Flip only the imaginary sign.

T1.text: Remember this. Keep the real part, flip the sign of the imaginary part.

D1.text: Now the magic from the hook. Why do the i's vanish?

D2.text: Step one. Add z and z bar. Real parts add, and imaginary parts add.

D3.text: Step two. Plus i b and minus i b cancel. What is left is two a, a real number.

D4.text: Step three. Multiply z by z bar. x plus y, times x minus y, is x squared minus y squared.

D5.text: Step four. i squared is minus one. So minus i squared b squared turns into plus b squared.

D6.text: So z times z bar is a squared plus b squared. Always real, never negative. For three plus two i: nine plus four, thirteen.

W2.text: Find the complex number z, if z plus two times z bar equals nine minus four i.

W3.text: Step one. Let z be x plus i y, with x and y real. Then z bar is x minus i y.

W4.text: Step two. Collect: x plus two x is three x, and i y minus two i y is minus i y.

W5.text: Step three. Equate real parts. Three x equals nine, so x is three.

W6.text: Step four. Equate imaginary parts. Minus y equals minus four, so y is four.

W7.text: So z is three plus four i. Check: three plus four i, plus six minus eight i, is nine minus four i.

X2.text: Solve: one plus i, times x, plus one minus i, times y, equals two plus four i. Many students write x is two, y is four.

X3.text: But x and y sit inside both parts. Collect first: x plus y is two, and x minus y is four. So x is three, and y is minus one.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main and JEE Advanced, as equations in z and z bar. And in PUC board exams, as direct questions.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Find the sum of the real parts of every element of S. Pause and solve.

A2.text: Write z as x plus i y. Real part: x squared minus y squared plus x. Imaginary part: y times two x minus one.

A3.text: Both parts must be zero. So y is zero, or x is one half.

A4.text: If y is zero, z is zero or minus one. If x is one half, y squared is three quarters: two more solutions.

A5.text: Real parts: zero, minus one, one half and one half. They add up to zero.
